en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Mother Deer, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Buddha said: "In the past, there was a herd of several hundred deer that followed water and grass, encroaching upon human settlements."
In that village, the king went out on a hunt, and the deer were consequently scattered in all directions.
There was one pregnant doe who fled alone; pursued, hungry, and exhausted, she lost her companions and was filled with sorrow.

At that time, she gave birth to two sons; leaving them behind as she went out to seek food, she became terrified and lost her way, mistakenly falling into a hunter's snare. She cried out piteously, wishing to escape, but was unable to free herself.
Hearing the sound, the hunter went to investigate; seeing the deer, he was filled with joy and moved forward, intending to kill it.
The deer then prostrated itself, pleading for mercy and explaining:
"I have recently given birth to two fawns who are still small and ignorant; they are just beginning to emerge from their state of confusion and do not yet know east from west."
I beg for a brief moment’s leave to return for a short while to see my son, to show him water and grass so that he may live, and to part from him with the two other sons in full mourning.
My life, long or short, is now at its end!
I pray that you will grant me your compassionate forgiveness and extend your pity to one such as I.
If I am moved by your mercy to see my son once more, it would be something for which even a deer or a beast could not repay.
"Heaven blesses those of virtue, and blessings flow upon them without limit.
As for the appointed time of my dispatch, I shall not violate my sworn pledge; I shall proceed to death immediately, and even in this animal form, I have no regrets."

At that time, the hunter, hearing what the deer said, was both startled and amazed; his hair stood on end as he marveled at its extraordinary ability to speak and its discernment beyond human emotion. He immediately asked the deer:
"Are you a malevolent spirit, or a tree deity of the mountains and forests?"
"You have attained freedom from delusion; you merely borrow this form.
Tell me the truth so that I may understand its cause.
The deer then replied:
"Due to the sins of greed and cruelty in my previous lives, I have received this deer body.

Because I think of you with a sincere heart, I am able to speak; I am not a ghost or a demon. I only ask that you recognize my plight and show me compassion: release me while I live, and let me return to death. I shall be content with what I have been spared."
Upon hearing this, the hunter placed greater trust in his words; yet, harboring greed in his heart, he was unwilling to listen and said to the deer:
"If all people of the world lack sincerity, how much more so you, a mere beast?"
I cherish my child and spare my own body, yet I still seek to remain alive; having departed from death, how could there be a time for returning?
The King’s command is urgent, and I fear he will surely learn of this; I shall be held guilty for losing the deer and incur even heavier retribution.
"Though my heart cannot bear it, I have no choice in the matter; I shall never let you go.
At that time, the deer was terrified and replied with bitter words:
"Though a deer is but a lowly beast, I would die gladly without regret. If you grant me a period of time to return, how could I dare disobey your command?"
When a person receives the retribution for their transgressions, they can only beg for a temporary extension of their lifespan, planted by their merits.
To depart would mean the survival of my son; to remain would mean his death. Grant me leave to go and return; let the spirit verify my words.
What is there to regret in my death? Yet how could I violate my heart’s conviction?
I look back with deep concern for my two sons; it is for this reason that I am so earnest.
If they do not know their mother in life, each shall surely perish; to sacrifice my own life to preserve my sons would extinguish three agonizing pains at once.
The mother deer lowered her head and cried out, speaking these verses:
"My body is that of a deer, Wandering and feeding in the forest thickets;
Born of low station, I am greedy for life, And cannot thus surrender my death."
Now I have come into your snare, willingly accepting the blade and the chopping block;
I do not begrudge this foul-smelling body, for I pity only my two children.
It was only because in my previous lives I was violent and cruel, lacking in sincerity.
Lacking faith in the suffering of birth and death, and failing to distinguish clearly between sin and merit,
one commits evil and thereby invites retribution; now receiving the form of a beast,
if I am granted but a moment’s life, I shall never violate my covenant of faith.
Thereupon, the hunter heard the sound of the deer’s plaintive appeal and marveled at its extraordinary nature!
Yet, driven by greed for gain and intent on accomplishing his purpose, he did not wish to release it. He immediately addressed the deer, rebuking and censuring him, saying:

“You are full of clever artifice and devoid of substance; you are treacherous and difficult to trust. Your empty flourishes are manifold and your guile is not of one kind. You have invaded and ravaged the lives of living beings and violated the crops of men; now, by virtue of your crimes, you have cast yourself into my snare.”

"I shall now kill you and send you to provide food for the King's kitchen. There is no need for you to lie and deceive me in hopes of escape; who, fearing death and cherishing their own life, would be able to sacrifice it?
For a human being, even without food, it is difficult to predict how long they will live, let alone for a beast."
"Since my life is entirely forfeit and death cannot be avoided, when could there ever be a time for my return?
I must simply face my death; you shall never let me go.

At that moment, the deer remembered her fawn and feared it would be seized. She knelt down on both knees, lowered her head, and wept with tears as she lamented with mournful cries, speaking these verses once more:
"Though my body is that of a deer and I am ignorant of benevolence and righteousness,
how could I receive your compassionate grace and depart without ever returning?"
I would rather endure the pain of being torn apart than exist in falsehood;
grieving for my two children’s destitution, I beg for a brief moment’s leave.
The sins of past lives manifest naturally, and thus one receives the body of an animal.
Because I am not trusted by others, misfortune and calamity naturally follow;
yet this also beckons my future. If I wish to escape the form of an animal, I shall bare my liver and reveal my sincerity; I pray you, hear my solemn vow.
If there are evil people in the world who incite strife and discord among the bhikṣu-saṃgha,
destroy stūpas and ruin Buddhist temples, or kill those who uphold the precepts;
who commit rebellion and harm their parents, brothers, wives, and children;
If I do not return, my transgression shall be greater than this.
It is the ultimate sin in all the world; even when the kalpa ends, the calamity shall not cease.
One will be tossed about and further scorched and boiled, passing from that place back to this one.
"You should consider how grave and heavy this is; the suffering you shall endure will have no end.
If I do not return, my transgression will be even greater than this.
At that time, the hunter heard the deer's words again, and his heart was moved with even greater trepidation. He then withdrew and sighed, saying:

"I observe only that all the people of this world, having received the blessings of their past lives and been born as humans, are yet deluded and ignorant, dark in their folly; they turn their backs on gratitude and lack righteousness, being neither loyal nor filial, neither faithful nor benevolent; they are greedy, cruel, and devoid of the Way, resorting to deception and falsehood merely to preserve themselves, unaware of impermanence and unable to distinguish the Three Honored Ones."

The deer is but a beast, yet its earnest words of parting and its sincere oaths of pledge are no different from those of a human; its feelings reveal its true sincerity as if clearly manifest. Observing these signs, one may examine its heart.
He then went forward, untied the snare, and released the deer.

Thereupon, the mother deer emerged from the trap and departed; she looked back as she ran toward her fawn’s location, lowered her head to sniff him, and licked his body. Alternating between joy and sorrow, she lingered and paced about, sighing and wailing as she spoke these verses:
"All meetings of affection and love Arise entirely from the convergence of causes and conditions."
Union is followed by separation; impermanence makes it difficult to endure for long.
Now that I am your mother, I constantly fear I shall not preserve myself;
living in this world is full of dread, for life is like dew upon the grass.

Thereupon, having spoken these verses, the doe took her two fawns into the forest thickets; she provided them with separate food and grain, pointed out excellent water and grass, and instructed them with earnest exhortation, teaching them the way of life.
Reflecting on his son’s solitude, tears fell like rain; with a sorrowful cry of lamentation, he spoke these verses of parting:
“In past lives I practiced deception, I incurred debts through attachment and love, I ravaged the lives of many beings, And I stole for myself while inciting others to kill.”
The body follows like a shadow; today you shall receive its consequences.
Having exhausted the old, do not create the new; you must return to meet that appointed time.
To oppose the Buddha and disbelieve the Dharma, to turn one's back on and violate the precepts of one’s teacher and father—this is the path of ruin.
Driven by greed and insatiable desire, I let my passions run wild and indulged in delusion.
As retribution for these sins, I have become an animal; I must serve as food for others.
I do not dare harbor resentment within myself, and until the end of my life, I shall no longer deceive.
Greedy and seeking through unrighteous means, having committed killing and theft in previous lives,
one is born repeatedly as a beast, pursued by the consequences of past karma.
Bound by fetters and facing death, one is filled with terror and lacks the will to live.
Heeding the words of the Triple Gem, he saw that he must sever all affection.
"This morning my journey met with misfortune; I have mistakenly fallen into the snare of a hunter.
I am now about to be butchered and dismembered, suffering the retribution of past karma."
I recall how you came seeking my compassion; now you must return to face death.
Out of pity for you two young orphans, I urge you to sustain yourselves through your own efforts.
When traveling, rely upon your kindred; when resting, rely upon the multitude.
When eating, one should proceed with companions; when lying down, one should wake up with alertness.
Be careful not to travel alone, like food being carried along the roadside.
Once words are spoken, there may be a final parting; having gone to death, one does not return.

At that time, having spoken these verses, the mother deer parted from her offspring in death; she lingered there for a second and a third time, bowing her head and looking up, uttering cries of poignant grief, and then turned her back and departed.

The two children cried out in lamentation, weeping with longing and affection as they pursued him from behind. Exhausted, they fell down and then rose again, wailing piteously and speaking these verses of complaint:
"Out of greed and longing for affection, I was born as a son to my mother;
Just as I first came to receive this physical form, I received the lowly body of a beast."
How could I have seen my mother abandoned, her life severed and she passing away here?
Grieving for my mother, my sorrow was absolute; I begged to die along with her.
I reflect that since my birth, I have not even known east from west.
Reflecting on our mother’s compassion for us, we ought to repay the kindness of her nursing us.
How could we bear to part from her forever, never to exist again?
Thinking of the suffering our mother endures for our sake, we find no solace in living on alone.
Lacking merit, one receives this animal form; with meager blessings, calamities and harms arrive.
Having begun in delusion, one shall soon meet with abandonment and solitude.
All who are born must die; sooner or later, one shall come to that end.
"The poverty and distress of this day / Shall be shared with my mother at the same time.

Having spoken these verses, the fawn’s mother was overcome with grief; she lowered her head and wailed, lamenting and sighing in sorrowful resentment. Turning her head back to look, she raised her voice in a mournful cry and said to her son:
"Return! Do not come!"
Since I have brought my affairs to an end, I shall meet death with a full lifespan;
let it not be that mother and child perish together through untimely calamity.
I die with a willing heart, for I grieve that you do not yet realize that in this world all is impermanent and everyone must eventually part.
"I am personally of meager fortune, and you have had no protection since birth; why do you grieve? It only serves to increase your anxieties and afflictions.
You should simply proceed quickly and settle this debt today."
The mother deer cried out again, speaking this verse for her child:
"In the past, I sat bound by craving and attachment; Now I have received this wretched animal body.
All born in this world must die; There is no escape from the suffering that ends not."
"Restrain your mind and depart from greed; only then will you find great peace.
It is better to die with utmost sincerity than to live a life of deceitful danger.

Thereupon, Ruru, hearing his mother’s verses, felt even deeper sorrow and longing. He followed her cries and weeping until he reached the trap. Searching here and there, he finally saw the hunter lying beneath a tree.
The doe went directly to his side, lowered her head, and cried out loudly to awaken the hunter, speaking in verse:
"Though my devotion was sincere and complete, I shall spend the rest of my life as a beast.
Having seen you release me, I dare not linger; I return instead to the blade and the chopping block."
The deer that was released just now has now returned to face its death;
though you showed such kindness to this lowly beast, it has been granted the sight of bidding farewell to its two fawns.
As you prepare to depart, show it water and grass, and for its sake, speak of the suffering of impermanence.
"Though I perish today without remainder, I dare not forget his kindness.

At that time, the hunter heard the deer’s cry as it spoke these words of sincerity and faith; startled awake, he rose immediately, his heart moved with awe, compassion arising from within him before his mouth could utter a word.
The deer then lowered its head, knelt on both knees before the hunter, and with joy addressed him, offering thanks in verse:
"O Benevolent One, you have just now released me; Your virtue is as vast as heaven and earth.
A lowly beast has been nurtured by your compassion; I cannot contain my feelings of gratitude."
All things are entirely impermanent; joyfully accepting this truth, I have brought death into accord with my faith.
Having extinguished all opposing conditions and ended all causes and effects, my enmities are exhausted from this point forward.
Your benevolence and kindness are difficult to forget; how could I dare to violate the gratitude I owe you?
Though I decline with a million words of refusal, they are insufficient to repay your compassionate grace.
Only by maintaining pure sincerity can one receive blessings that return to the natural order;
today I am content to die, entrusting my son to your benevolent majesty.

Thereupon, the hunter was moved by his sincerity and immediately fell asleep; he again heard the deer recite verses, all in a most subtle and wondrous voice. His profound faith was further strengthened, and he abandoned life for death to fulfill his solemn oath.
The mother and child deer wept piteously as they followed one another to that spot.
"This deer's body must surely be no ordinary thing; among the people of the world I have seen, none can be compared to it."
"Though he possesses the body of a beast, his mind is like that of a divine spirit.
My own lack of virtue has led to long-standing cruelty.
This deer, however, establishes righteousness; his words are trustworthy and he does not fail his word. He may serve as a clear teacher; I bow my head to receive his instruction."
"How could I ever again dare to harbor a heart of malice or harm toward you?
At that moment, the hunter became solemn and reverent; he apologized and dismissed the deer, speaking these verses:
"The divine deer is as true as heaven; Your vows and aspirations are vast."
Now my heart trembles with fear; how could I dare commit such an act of rebellion?
It would be better to take my own lowly life and have my wife and children cut limb from limb;
how could I bear to turn toward the seed of heaven and harbor thoughts of harming the divine spirit?
After the hunter had spoken this verse, he sent the deer away with a heart of loving-kindness, repeatedly taking his leave and expressing regret while reproaching himself.

Seeing that he was being dismissed, the deer went out to her fawn; seeing his mother from afar, the fawn, having been able to escape and return, ran toward her with great speed, leaping and crying out in grief.

The mother and child found one another; both were joyful and delighted. One lowered its head and the other raised it, their voices crying out in harmony. Having experienced sorrow and now receiving life, and having received this great kindness, the deer immediately looked up and thanked the hunter, speaking these verses:
"Living as a lowly beast in this world, I ought to have been served in the kitchen.
Had I been slaughtered and placed upon the carving board this very moment, I would have had no leisure to bid farewell to my two children."
"O Deva and humans, you hold me dear; I have further received your pardon and grace.
The accumulated blessings of this virtue are immeasurable, Beyond what can be fully recounted by word.

At that time, having spoken these verses of gratitude, the mother deer led her two offspring back to the deep forest. She joined her herd and called to her companions, wandering and gathering with them, finding refuge in the grassy marshes and dwelling in peace upon the steep mountains.
The hunter, following behind, reflected deeply within himself:
"This deer was but a mere beast, yet its integrity and faithfulness protected its body; having escaped, it is now saved, and those who see it will offer praise."
"What is so vast about my cruelty that it has expanded my heart to this?
Immediately, he awakened from his delusion, dispersed his thoughts, and returned to benevolence; he cast away his bow, destroyed his snares, and no longer harbored any intent to kill.

He went to a temple and requested an audience with a śramaṇa; bowing his head to the ground, he took refuge and presented his case, pledging to follow the compassionate dharma and dedicating his will to the true and correct path.
He then went to inform the king, recounting the deer’s words in full detail.
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with joy and marveled in astonishment:
"The deer possesses righteousness, whereas I am even more greedy and cruel.
Furthermore, this deer’s wisdom deeply penetrates the teachings; he knows to revere the Triple Gem."
"Our nation is in a state of decline and obscurity, yet we follow those deluded words.
It would truly be right to abandon them in order to preserve our eternal security.

Thus, throughout the entire country, there was no one who did not hear and know that the conduct of the beast had been proven by manifest evidence; the transformation of the Great Way was revealed, leaving nothing hidden.
Thereupon, the king immediately summoned his ministers and issued a proclamation to the people:

"In my ignorance, I failed to distinguish between truth and falsehood; I accepted the teachings of heterodox masters, spoke with fear of false deities, performed demonic sacrifices devoid of the Way, and treated sentient beings with cruelty.
I am not even equal to a deer, which clearly recognizes the Triple Gem."
"From this day forward, throughout the entire kingdom, I shall lead the people to abolish those heterodox sects and cause them all to return to the True and Righteous.
He then went to the Buddhist temples to request ordination from the holy assembly, hoping that in future lives he might long obtain its blessings.
The ministers, officials, and the people, both great and small, all placed their faith in the Triple Gem and observed the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds.
Within three years, the nation became prosperous and peaceful, and the people were long-lived and happy; such was the protection bestowed by the Deer King.
The Buddha said to the venerable Ānanda:

"It was solely through my skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and the practice of benevolence throughout successive kalpas that I have thus inspired faith in sentient beings whom I have saved with kindness.
At that time, the mother deer was none other than myself."
The two sons were Rāhula and the son of the mother of Zhu-li;
the king was Śāriputra; and the hunter was Ānanda.
"The subject from the realm who ran to inform the King was Devadatta.

Having spoken thus, the Buddha emitted a great radiance from his calves that shone throughout the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and the ten directions, illuminating a thousand Buddha-fields in each.

Wherever my light reaches, there appear transformed seats for the sons of the Dharma-guides and precious lotus flowers; some manifest as bhikṣu Dharma-preachers in physical form, some as kings or the sons of elders, some as commoners or the masses appearing in humble and lowly forms, and some as human beings born as beasts—each using their light to guide and lead others by preaching the Dharma.

At that time, the merit of the doe’s vow and pledge, which had been expounded as a teaching for the Dharma, entered their hearts through the sound of the Dharma; there was none who did not believe and accept it, and all returned to the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

The Buddha immediately turned his radiance back, equally receiving and illuminating the entire Jambudvīpa, causing it to be thoroughly pervaded; those who were touched by this light attained a sense of peace and security.

At that time, there were eight hundred bhikṣus in the assembly whose minds were set upon the four paths and who had realized the traces of the Way. Hearing it said that the mother deer, even among the animals, had conceived the Great Resolve and attained the Way through faith, they were moved to realization and underwent a transformation of heart, immediately repenting their former ways.

They came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying: "We vow to establish a firm pledge for the path of the bodhisattva. May the Buddha graciously grant us his aid and benefit; we shall build our practice to bear the burden of sentient beings, rescuing and saving all until death, never departing from them. Immediately, we attain the saṃnāha-saṃnaddha, the armor of the great vow."
At that time, Ānanda adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"These bhikṣus were ensnared by delusion regarding the Mahāyāna and did not accept the True Dharma; yet now they have attained awakening and realized the Dharma—how swift it is for them to leave the abyss and leap over the moat!"
"This is truly not something that those of minor paths can believe or clarify.
We have doubts regarding this great assembly; we only pray that the World-Honored One will explain its causes and conditions so as to dispel them for the future!
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Ānanda!
Your question is most timely.”
This is a continuation of former recognition, not something newly created now.

These bhikṣus were formerly the people of the kingdom of Mṛgadāva; they faithfully accepted the king’s command and reverently followed the Three Jewels. Because they added [the practice of] "deer-like" [gentleness], they were immediately moved by resonance, and all formed the aspiration for unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment.

During the intervening period of delusion and darkness, he no longer practiced; although he encountered me and became a śramaṇa, he suddenly abandoned his original vow and became confused regarding the Mahāyāna.

Now, having heard my account of the beginning and end of his previous lives, his knots of doubt have been untied and he has attained the peace of non-conceptualization; this is brought about by the consciousness-spirit of his past destiny.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, eight hundred bhikṣus all attained the stage of *avaivartika*;

among the eight thousand people in the assembly of Mallas, their minds were liberated through realization, they abandoned heedless conduct, and all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, attaining entry into faith and immediately obtaining the tranquil concentration of non-conceptualization (*animitta-samādhi*);
and seventy-two million devas, nāgas, and worldlings all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"When I was in the form of an animal, because I did not forget the Bodhisattva’s heart of vast salvation, I continued to practice guidance and benefit until the present day; yet, for the sake of sentient beings, my diligent toil has been boundless.
Even if there were but a single person who had lost their fundamental nature and sunk into the flow of suffering without being rescued, I would never abandon them."

All those who seek peace and wish to attain these merits and swiftly achieve Buddhahood should, with complete sincerity of heart, take refuge in and believe in the Triple Gem, never abandoning them throughout successive lifetimes.
"Just as I manifest parinirvāṇa today, it is brought about by the power of sincere faith. Ānanda!
You should receive and uphold this sutra, proclaiming it widely so that it does not perish."
Ānanda immediately stepped forward, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, and received, upheld, and recited it.
Thus ends the *Mṛgī-mātṛ-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha.
